safetyNote: Poisonous: do not eat. Entoloma sinuatum causes severe nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, sometimes with dehydration and temporary changes in liver tests. Symptoms may begin hours after a meal; the Belgian Poison Centre reports 3–8 hours and sometimes hospital care is needed. The responsible toxins are poorly characterized. Contact a poison centre or urgent medical service after suspected ingestion and retain mushroom or meal remains for identification.

sections.title: Large pale cap
sections.text: The broad, fleshy cap is often 6–20 cm across. It begins convex with an inturned edge, then spreads out and may develop a low blunt central bump and an irregular wavy margin. Colour varies from ivory or cream to pale grey, grey-beige or yellowish buff. The surface is smooth to finely silky with subtle radial fibres and is not conspicuously grooved at the rim.

sections.title: Gills, stem and spore deposit
sections.text: The broad gills are attached near the stem with a notch, sometimes appearing almost free. Young gills are cream to yellowish, often butter-yellow, then become salmon-pink as the spores mature; the yellow phase varies and is not universal. The solid white to cream stem is sturdy, usually cylindrical or swollen toward the base, and has no ring or volva. The spore deposit is pink; microscopic spores are angular, unlike the smooth oval spores of many lookalikes.

sections.title: Flesh, habitat and season
sections.text: The thick white flesh may smell mealy, especially when cut, but the smell can be weak or unpleasant in older mushrooms. The species fruits on soil among broadleaf trees such as oak and beech, often in open woodland, edges or parks, commonly on clay or limestone-rich ground. In Europe it is mainly seen from late summer through autumn, with local climate shifting the season.

sections.title: Confusions and poisoning
sections.text: Young fruit bodies with still pale gills may be confused with Calocybe gambosa, Clitopilus prunulus or other pale edible-looking mushrooms; older specimens may be mistaken for the clouded agaric, Clitocybe nebularis. The combination of a large pale cap, notched gills changing from yellowish to pink, ringless robust stem and pink spore deposit is useful, but no one sign proves safe identification. The Belgian Poison Centre describes a severe gastrointestinal syndrome, usually resolving over several days, with dehydration sometimes requiring admission and monitoring of liver tests.

traits: Large fleshy ivory to grey-beige cap, commonly 6–20 cm, with an inturned then wavy edge
Smooth to faintly silky cap with subtle radial fibres and occasional blunt central bump
Broad notched or nearly free gills, cream-yellow when young and salmon-pink at maturity
Robust white to cream stem, sometimes swollen at base, without ring or volva
Thick white flesh; mealy odour may be weak or turn unpleasant with age
Pink spore deposit; broadleaf woodland on often calcareous or clay soil, chiefly late summer to autumn
